summary: Shares experience from using ISO 8613, the Office Document Architecture (ODA), to translate multimedia information. It is meant for implementors considering ODA as a format for multimedia mail and file exchange. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC shares experience from a project that used Office Document Architecture to exchange multimedia documents. It explains why an application profile is needed to connect ODA's abstract structures to the concepts used by applications.

subtitle: Experience using Office Document Architecture to exchange multimedia documents.

tldr.problem: Implementers considering ODA for multimedia exchange needed practical information about using the abstract document format.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC summarizes the EXPRES project's work investigating ODA for sending research proposals by electronic mail and points to a book describing the results.
tldr.outcome: It records experience intended to help others considering ODA as an interchange medium; the memo does not specify a standard.

today: RFC 1197 is Informational. It records experience using ODA and does not define a standard.

sections.title: What ODA Represents
sections.content:
Office Document Architecture (ODA), ISO 8613 and CCITT T.410, represents documents containing multifont text, raster images, and geometric graphics. The RFC says ODA had been specified for use in related standards such as X.400.

ODA is abstract and defines structures such as composite logical object classes rather than common document items such as paragraphs. To use it as an interchange medium, a document application profile (DAP) must define common entities and map between ODA and the systems exchanging documents.
sections.plainLanguage: ODA can represent text and images, but its abstract building blocks do not directly match familiar document parts. A DAP defines common items and how to map them between systems.

sections.title: The EXPRES Project
sections.content:
The National Science Foundation funded the EXPRES project. Teams at Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Michigan worked with McDonnell-Douglas Aerospace Information Systems, NIST, and Interleaf to investigate using ODA for submitting research proposals to the National Science Foundation by electronic mail.

The project based its strategies on the NIST DAP and features in the Andrew, Diamond, and Interleaf systems. The RFC directs readers to a book documenting the experience.
sections.plainLanguage: EXPRES brought together several organizations to test ODA for sending research proposals by email. The RFC summarizes the work and points to a fuller account.

sections.title: Purpose and Limitations
sections.content:
RFC 1197 shares experience for implementers considering ODA in an open-systems environment. It is an informational memo and does not specify a standard.

The RFC's disclaimer says the referenced book represents the authors' opinions, not the policies of the organizations named in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo shares implementation experience rather than defining a standard. It also distinguishes the authors' opinions from the policies of their organizations.

references.text: Rosenberg, J., Sherman, M., Marks, A., and Akkerhuis, J., "Multi-media Document Translation: ODA and the EXPRES Project", Springer-Verlag, 1991.
